messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Vignette for Mr. Vinay Patel Vinay Patel is a 22-year-old South Eastern Asian male who has been struggling with the aftermath of a traumatic natural disaster that occurred several months ago. Born and raised in Houston, Texas, Vinay now works as a UX Designer at a tech startup. His trauma began on a day like any other until a severe hurricane made landfall, transforming his city into a chaotic landscape. The storm brought torrential rains and winds that destroyed homes and left many injured or displaced. Vinay was at work when the disaster struck. He recalled feeling overwhelmed by the chaos outside his office window—trees uprooted, power lines down, and water flooding streets in mere minutes. Despite efforts to evacuate orderly, panic set in as people rushed to get to higher ground. Vinay found himself caught in a surge of panic-stricken individuals, jostling for space on a stairway that became dangerously crowded. In the midst of this chaos, he fell and hit his head, leaving him with lingering neck pain. Since the disaster, Vinay has been plagued by vivid triggers. The persistent neck pain often brings back the memory of falling and the fear he felt in those moments. Even more unsettling are the times when he feels physically unwell—a sensation that transports him back to the nausea-inducing fear during the storm's peak. These sensations make him acutely aware of his body, as if it is constantly signaling danger. Vinay’s memories of the event have taken on a surreal quality. At times, the memory seems so extreme and unbelievable that he questions whether it truly happened to him. During moments when the trauma resurfaces, he can vividly taste the metal-like flavor from the air during the storm. He also experiences intense emotions without any clear image or context, leaving him feeling overwhelmed by a sense of loss and fear. These triggers have deeply affected Vinay’s daily life as a UX Designer. Working in an open office space means constant exposure to potential stressors, such as sudden loud noises that can mimic the sounds of the storm. He has started avoiding certain areas of his workplace where he feels particularly vulnerable, leading to increased isolation from colleagues and decreased productivity. Vinay's distrust of others has grown significantly since the event. He finds it difficult to trust even close friends and colleagues, believing that people are not what they seem. This suspicion has led him to withdraw socially, feeling more isolated and disconnected from those around him. The sense of not belonging anywhere—neither at work nor among his peers—has compounded his feelings of isolation. Vinay’s relationship with his family has also been strained. He avoids talking about the disaster, preferring silence over recounting the traumatic events. This withdrawal has led to misunderstandings and a growing distance between him and his loved ones. What finally brought Vinay to seek help was the realization that his symptoms were becoming too overwhelming to manage on his own. He feared that he might lose his job due to decreased performance and felt increasingly hopeless about ever feeling normal again. Despite these fears, there is also a flicker of hope within him—that with support and guidance, he can regain control over his life and find a way to reintegrate into the world without constant dread. In therapy, Vinay hopes to understand why his body and mind continue to relive that harrowing day. He wants to learn how to manage his triggers better and rebuild trust in others so he can feel connected again. His journey towards healing will require navigating through these complex emotions and memories, but he is determined to find a path forward.
